paragraphs: A model can produce the right answer to a reasoning problem while misunderstanding the concepts behind its inputs. The paper studies these reasoning shortcuts: situations where success on a downstream task does not require associating the correct concepts with complex data. This matters because accurate answers alone can give an incomplete picture of a model’s interpretability and generalization.

The authors introduce rsbench, a benchmark suite for examining this mismatch systematically. It provides customizable tasks affected by reasoning shortcuts, together with shared metrics for measuring concept quality. It also introduces formal verification procedures for assessing whether learning tasks admit these shortcuts, bringing a more explicit check of the problem structure into evaluation.

Experiments with rsbench show that obtaining high-quality concepts remains difficult for both purely neural and neuro-symbolic models. The contribution is therefore an evaluation resource that separates successful task completion from sound concept learning. Its findings support examining what a model has learned internally alongside whether its final answers are correct.
neurips-2024-a-neuro-symbolic-benchmark-.tldr: rsbench evaluates whether models learn the intended concepts or solve reasoning tasks through shortcuts.

paragraphs: Language models trained on antibody sequences could help antibody discovery, but evaluating their usefulness requires labeled examples of molecular interactions. The paper addresses this data shortage with resources for studying VHH antibodies. Its focus is whether sequence representations support predicting binding to SARS-CoV-2 targets, making a specific biological interaction the basis for evaluation.

The first resource, AVIDa-SARS-CoV-2, contains interaction data obtained from two alpacas immunized with SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins. It pairs diverse VHH sequences with binding or non-binding labels for 12 viral mutants, including Delta and Omicron. The second resource, VHHCorpus-2M, contains more than two million VHH sequences intended for language-model pretraining.

The authors benchmark binding prediction using VHHBERT, pretrained on their sequence corpus, alongside existing general protein and antibody-specific language models. The stated findings establish the interaction dataset as a useful benchmark for assessing representations used in binding prediction. Together, the resources provide both material for learning antibody representations and labeled interactions for testing what those representations capture.
neurips-2024-a-sars-cov-2-interaction-da.tldr: Two new VHH datasets support pretraining antibody language models and evaluating their SARS-CoV-2 binding predictions.

paragraphs: Existing language models can contain complementary knowledge, creating an opportunity to combine their strengths for clinical text. This paper introduces a teacher-teacher framework that enables mutual learning between two already available models. Its starting point is reuse: the framework does not require developing a new language model or continuing the pretraining of an existing one.

The central component is LINE, a lightweight knowledge alignment module. It harmonizes the two teachers’ knowledge within a shared representation space. This common space is intended to make their complementary information useful together when representing clinical notes, giving the framework a focused mechanism for combining what the models already know.

The clinical setting matters because detailed notes are subject to privacy considerations and stringent handling requirements. The trained LINE module captures critical information using highly de-identified data, and validation and downstream tasks demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. These results support knowledge alignment as a practical way to improve clinical representations while working with the restricted form of text described in the study.
neurips-2024-a-teacher-teacher-framework.tldr: A lightweight alignment module combines complementary knowledge from two existing models to represent highly de-identified clinical notes.

paragraphs: Training deep spiking neural networks with backpropagation through time can require substantial memory and computation because learning follows activity across time. This paper builds on evidence that firing rates are a primary form of information captured by this training procedure. That observation motivates simplifying the learning calculation around the representations the network is already using.

The proposed rate-based backpropagation focuses on averaged dynamics and reduces reliance on detailed temporal derivatives. This produces a simpler computational graph, lowering the resources needed for training. The authors support the gradient approximation relative to backpropagation through time through both theoretical analysis and empirical observations, connecting the computational shortcut to its learning behavior.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and CIFAR10-DVS report performance comparable to backpropagation-through-time counterparts and better results than leading efficient training techniques. The findings show that exploiting rate-based representations can reduce training complexity while preserving performance in the evaluated settings. This makes the approach relevant to scaling spiking-network training under constrained memory and computation.
neurips-2024-advancing-training-efficien.tldr: Rate-based backpropagation reduces spiking-network training costs while achieving performance comparable to backpropagation through time in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot learning asks a model trained on a large source dataset to adapt to a different domain using very few examples. This paper investigates Vision Transformers in that setting, especially when the source and target differ substantially. It examines whether their learned attention remains useful after this change in the data.

The authors observe that multiplying attention by a temperature improves target-domain performance in their experiments, even when a zero temperature makes the attention map uniform. They interpret this behavior as a remedy for ineffective target-domain attention produced by the query-key mechanism under large domain gaps. The observation links a simple attention adjustment to a specific source of transfer difficulty.

Building on that interpretation, the proposed method discourages learning in query-key parameters while encouraging learning in the remaining parameters. Experiments on four cross-domain few-shot datasets support the explanation and report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The result suggests that controlling which transformer components adapt can improve transfer when only a small target training set is available.
neurips-2024-attention-temperature-matte.tldr: Adjusting attention temperature and restraining query-key learning improve Vision Transformer transfer across domains in few-shot experiments.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks corresponding vertices in related graphs. This paper studies correlated stochastic block models with two balanced communities, where community structure complicates identifying those correspondences. The authors provide the first efficient matching algorithm for this setting, addressing a case in which the hidden community partition cannot always be recovered exactly from either graph alone.

When average degree grows logarithmically with the number of vertices, the algorithm matches all but a vanishing fraction of vertices with high probability if the edge correlation satisfies s² > α, where α is approximately 0.338. It extends a method based on counts of tree-shaped subgraphs called chandeliers, while handling additional errors arising from estimated community membership.

The authors also extend the approach to efficient exact matching whenever exact matching is information-theoretically possible in the studied setting. As an application, they obtain exact community recovery from multiple correlated graphs in parameter regimes where one graph cannot provide enough information. These results connect efficient correspondence finding with the additional recoverable structure available across related graphs.
neurips-2024-efficient-graph-matching-fo.tldr: The paper gives efficient graph-matching algorithms for correlated two-community models, with conditional guarantees for near-complete and exact recovery.

paragraphs: A neural network’s loss landscape describes how prediction error changes as its parameters move. Beyond whether a valley is flat or sharp, its two sides can behave differently. This paper investigates that asymmetry and asks which aspects of training and visualization influence the shape observed around a converged network.

The study considers datasets, architectures, initialization, and hyperparameters that affect the final parameters, as well as the size and direction of perturbations used for one-dimensional visualizations. Its main observation is that sign consistency between the perturbation and the converged parameters is a critical indicator of valley symmetry. Theoretical insights involving ReLU and softmax offer explanations for this relationship.

The authors connect the finding to model fusion. They report that the effectiveness of interpolating independently trained models strongly correlates with the models’ sign consistency ratio. They also introduce sign alignment during federated learning as an approach to parameter alignment. The work therefore links a geometric observation about loss landscapes to how separate models can be combined.
neurips-2024-exploring-and-exploiting-th.tldr: Parameter sign consistency helps explain asymmetric loss valleys and is associated with how effectively separately trained models can be combined.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities encompass optimization problems such as minimization and min-max learning. Methods that use higher-order derivative information can have expensive iterations because they demand precise derivative calculations. This paper studies how inaccurate Jacobians affect second-order methods, making the accuracy of derivative information an explicit part of the analysis.

For smooth, monotone problems, the authors establish a lower bound that depends on the level of Jacobian error and propose an optimal algorithm for that setting. When derivatives are exact, the algorithm recovers the convergence rate of optimal exact second-order methods. This connects the approximate and exact cases within a common treatment rather than analyzing them as unrelated procedures.

The paper also introduces Quasi-Newton approximations to reduce the cost of an auxiliary problem that appears in globally convergent higher-order methods. With these updates, the method has a global sublinear convergence guarantee. A tensor extension handles inaccurate higher-order derivatives, and experiments support the theory. The contribution clarifies both what approximation costs in convergence and how it can make individual iterations cheaper.
neurips-2024-exploring-jacobian-inexactn.tldr: The paper characterizes how Jacobian errors affect second-order optimization and develops optimal and Quasi-Newton methods with stated convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Real-world graphs can contain different kinds of geometric structure, making a single representation space insufficient to capture all their complexity. This paper investigates how graph neural networks can learn from multiple geometries through knowledge distillation. The aim is to give a student model access to structural information represented differently by several teachers.

The framework mixes Euclidean and hyperbolic geometries when encoding graphs. Each teacher produces hint embeddings that capture distinct geometric properties. A structure-wise transfer module uses these embeddings in their respective geometric contexts, while a geometric optimization network addresses differences between their distributions. Together, these components organize how complementary teacher representations contribute to student training.

Experiments show that the framework captures graph topology more effectively and produces stronger student models than traditional distillation methods in the evaluated settings. Its model-agnostic design makes the contribution a way of transferring geometric knowledge across models. The findings support combining geometries during distillation when the graph’s structural diversity is difficult to express within one geometric space.
neurips-2024-geometry-awakening-cross-ge.tldr: A model-agnostic distillation framework combines Euclidean and hyperbolic teacher representations to improve graph student models.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular properties with machine learning depends heavily on labeled examples, yet producing biochemical annotations requires substantial effort. This paper tackles that shortage by helping a target model use large amounts of unlabeled molecular data. The central question is how to make those additional examples useful when their labels have not been established.

The proposed algorithm, InstructMol, measures the reliability of pseudo-labels: labels supplied by a model for otherwise unlabeled examples. This reliability assessment guides the target model’s use of the unlabeled data. The approach does not require knowledge transfer across multiple domains, avoiding the potential mismatch between pretraining and fine-tuning that motivates this aspect of the design.

The authors report high prediction accuracy on several real-world molecular datasets and out-of-distribution benchmarks. These findings support the usefulness of reliability-aware pseudo-label learning in the evaluated molecular prediction settings, including tests involving distribution shifts. The contribution centers on making better use of available unlabeled molecules when obtaining additional biochemical labels is laborious.
neurips-2024-instructor-inspired-machine.tldr: InstructMol assesses pseudo-label reliability to help molecular prediction models learn from large amounts of unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Supervised multimodal learning combines several forms of input to predict a target label. Useful information can come from relationships within one modality or from interactions across modalities. This paper argues that approaches concentrating exclusively on either kind of dependency may miss information needed for accurate prediction, and therefore may not be optimal in general.

The authors develop I2M2, a framework that captures and integrates both kinds of dependency. Their reasoning starts from a generative view in which the target is treated as a source of the modalities and their interactions. This perspective motivates representing the information each modality contributes individually together with the information available through their relationships.

Experiments use healthcare and vision-and-language datasets with state-of-the-art models. The reported results show better performance than traditional methods focused on only one dependency type. These findings support the framework’s central claim in the tested settings: multimodal prediction can benefit from jointly modeling individual sources of evidence and the interactions that connect them to the target.
neurips-2024-jointly-modeling-inter-intr.tldr: I2M2 improves multimodal prediction by jointly modeling label-related dependencies within modalities and across them.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing often collects only a few labels per example to control annotation costs, and those labels can be noisy. Related examples can help infer the underlying label, but existing neighborhood-based approaches assume the same number of neighbors for every example. This paper introduces KFNN to choose neighborhood size separately from each example’s attributes and noisy annotations.

KFNN first estimates a Mahalanobis distance distribution in the attribute space to describe how an example relates to the classes. It uses this information to refine the distribution derived from the example’s multiple noisy labels. A Kalman filter then reduces the influence of noise introduced by neighboring examples, and max-margin learning determines the neighborhood size.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over the other state-of-the-art algorithms evaluated, together with greater robustness across crowdsourcing scenarios. The method’s contribution is to make borrowing information from neighbors adaptive to the example. Its sequence of attribute-based refinement, noise filtering, and neighborhood selection addresses both sparse annotations and the uncertainty of neighboring evidence.
neurips-2024-kfnn-k-free-nearest-neighbo.tldr: KFNN infers labels from noisy crowdsourced annotations by filtering neighbor noise and adapting neighborhood size to each example.

paragraphs: Image captioning can serve as a way to pretrain visual representations, giving natural language a role in teaching models about images. This paper explores how that interface can also teach spatial information. LocCa extends caption-based pretraining with tasks that require the model to connect image content with where it appears.

The method adds bounding-box prediction and location-dependent captioning, both conditioned on image pixels. An encoder-decoder architecture handles these tasks together during pretraining. The design combines describing visual content with predicting its location, so the training objectives ask the model to extract information useful for both language descriptions and spatial reasoning about the image.

LocCa substantially improves on standard captioners for downstream localization and achieves state-of-the-art results on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg. At the same time, its performance on holistic image tasks remains comparable. The findings show that adding location-aware tasks can strengthen spatial representations without sacrificing the reported whole-image performance, supporting further use of natural language interfaces for varied visual pretraining objectives.
neurips-2024-locca-visual-pretraining-wi.tldr: LocCa adds location-aware tasks to image-captioning pretraining, improving localization while maintaining comparable whole-image task performance.

paragraphs: A function’s Jacobian describes how its outputs change under small changes to its inputs. Penalizing the Jacobian’s nuclear norm encourages the function to vary locally along only a few directions. This offers a useful form of regularization, but directly constructing a large Jacobian and computing its singular value decomposition is impractical for high-dimensional learning problems.

The paper develops a formulation tailored to composed functions, written as f = g ∘ h. The authors prove an equivalent penalty based on the average squared Frobenius norms of the component Jacobians. They then introduce a denoising-style approximation that removes the need to calculate those Jacobians explicitly, turning the theoretical formulation into a more practical training method.

The resulting approach is described as simple, efficient, and accurate, allowing the regularizer to scale to high-dimensional deep learning. An empirical study examines its behavior and applications in denoising and representation learning. The contribution is a computational route to encouraging low-rank local behavior without carrying out the expensive matrix calculations that originally defined the penalty.
neurips-2024-nuclear-norm-regularization.tldr: A composition-based formulation and denoising approximation make Jacobian nuclear-norm regularization practical for high-dimensional deep learning.

paragraphs: Structured state space models are linear dynamical systems used within networks such as S4 and Mamba. Unlike many neural-network components, they often use complex-valued parameters. This paper investigates why that choice can help, establishing formal differences between diagonal state space models parameterized with real numbers and those parameterized with complex numbers.

The first result concerns representation size: a complex model of moderate dimension can express all mappings of a real model, while a real model can need much greater dimension to express mappings of a complex one. The second concerns parameter magnitude. Even when a real model has enough dimensions, representing a given mapping typically requires exponentially large parameter values, creating a practical learning obstacle.

By contrast, the complex parameterization can express the mappings considered with moderate parameter values. Experiments corroborate these theoretical results. They also suggest that the theory might extend to selectivity, an additional architectural feature; that extension remains a possibility indicated by the experiments. The established results explain advantages in both representation size and parameter scale for diagonal models.
neurips-2024-provable-benefits-of-comple.tldr: The paper proves representation-size and parameter-magnitude advantages for complex over real diagonal state space models.

paragraphs: Understanding language-model training requires access to both the text and the decisions used to curate it. This paper identifies three obstacles to open model development: limited transparency, insufficient access to large quantities of quality data, and missing metadata or artifacts for analyzing and selecting that data. RedPajama supplies resources intended to address these connected problems.

RedPajama-V1 reproduces the LLaMA training dataset openly. RedPajama-V2 provides raw, unfiltered web text accompanied by quality signals and metadata. Together, the datasets contain more than 100 trillion tokens across multiple domains. The accompanying information gives users a basis for constructing filtered subsets and studying data selection, alongside access to the underlying text.

The authors analyze data quality through studies and ablations using decoder-only language models with up to 1.6 billion parameters. Their findings show that the quality signals can guide the creation of high-quality web-data subsets. The abstract also reports use of RedPajama in production language models, supporting its role as infrastructure for transparent dataset curation and model development.
neurips-2024-redpajama-an-open-dataset-f.tldr: RedPajama releases large open text datasets with curation signals that help researchers construct and study language-model training data.

paragraphs: Differentiable pruning searches for smaller networks using continuous masks, producing a soft version of the architecture during optimization. Deployment requires a discrete, hard network, and converting between the two can reduce representational capacity. This paper investigates that discretization gap and introduces S2HPruner, a structural pruning framework that addresses it during a single training stage.

During training, the method evaluates both the soft network and its corresponding hard network. The soft network supervises the hard network through knowledge distillation. A decoupled bidirectional distillation mechanism controls how learning signals flow: it blocks hard-to-soft weight updates while preserving the gradient associated with the mask. This lets mask optimization continue while protecting the soft network from the specified weight updates.

Experiments across multiple architectures on CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet report stronger pruning performance than existing methods without fine-tuning. Additional analysis experiments support the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution directly connects the architecture used for differentiable search with the discrete network that pruning ultimately produces, reducing the performance mismatch between them.
neurips-2024-s2hpruner-soft-to-hard-dist.tldr: S2HPruner uses controlled soft-to-hard distillation during pruning to reduce discretization losses and deliver strong results without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Point-cloud assembly seeks a rigid transformation that places one cloud correctly relative to another. The problem becomes difficult when the clouds do not overlap or start in arbitrary positions. This paper introduces BITR, a transformer designed around the transformation behavior of the task itself, with guarantees about how its output responds to changes in the inputs.

BITR uses SE(3) bi-equivariance: when the input clouds undergo rigid transformations, the predicted transformation changes accordingly. It first extracts features through an SE(3) × SE(3) transformer, then projects the learned feature into SE(3) to produce a rigid transformation. This structure supports handling non-overlapping clouds and guarantees robustness to their initial positions.

The authors also show theoretically that swap and scale equivariances can be incorporated, providing corresponding stability when the input order or scale changes. Practical experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines an assembly architecture with explicit transformation guarantees, tying the network’s behavior to geometric properties of the problem rather than leaving those properties solely to training.
neurips-2024-se-3-bi-equivariant-transfo.tldr: BITR assembles point clouds using geometric equivariance that guarantees consistent responses to rigid changes in their initial positions.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns agreement between predicted probabilities and observed binary outcomes. This paper asks how efficiently samples can distinguish perfect calibration from being at least a specified distance away. It frames that question as property testing, making both the amount of data required and the computational work part of the problem.

The key step reformulates an empirical smooth-calibration linear program as a minimum-cost flow problem on a specially structured graph. An exact dynamic-programming solver then runs in O(n log² n) time for n samples. The resulting calibration test is information-theoretically optimal and avoids the higher computational cost of applying general-purpose linear-programming solvers to the same formulation.

The authors also give faster algorithms for tolerant testing variants and sample-complexity lower bounds for alternative calibration measures. Experiments show that their testing formulation reflects standard notions of calibration and that the algorithms scale to large sample sizes. The work makes a rigorous calibration measure substantially more tractable while clarifying how the choice of measure affects testing requirements.
neurips-2024-testing-calibration-in-near.tldr: A structured flow formulation enables an information-theoretically optimal calibration test running in O(n log² n) time.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models activate specialized subnetworks, but their inference efficiency depends on how expert selection interacts with memory management and batching. This paper introduces Read-ME, a framework that converts pretrained dense language models into smaller expert models. Reusing a pretrained model avoids the cost of training the mixture-of-experts architecture from scratch.

Read-ME extracts experts using activation sparsity. It also examines redundancy in conventional layer-wise routing and introduces a pre-gating router separate from the expert backbone. Computing routing decisions ahead of time enables lookahead scheduling, expert-aware batching, and caching. The architecture and execution policies are therefore designed together to address both model computation and system-level overhead.

The reported comparisons with popular open-source dense models of similar scale show MMLU improvements of up to 10.1% and mean end-to-end latency improvements of up to 6.1%. These are reported upper-end gains rather than uniform benefits for every case. The findings support converting existing dense models and reorganizing routing as a combined approach to efficient inference in resource-constrained settings.
neurips-2024-textit-read-me-refactorizin.tldr: Read-ME converts dense language models into smaller expert models and separates routing to improve inference scheduling and reported performance.

paragraphs: Bounding boxes locate objects in autonomous-driving scenes but leave out detailed shape information. Occupancy representations can capture that geometry, yet high-resolution coverage of an entire large scene is computationally impractical. This paper concentrates occupancy modeling on foreground objects, which occupy only a small portion of the scene, to supplement boxes with finer geometric detail.

The authors contribute an object-centric occupancy dataset built through an automated pipeline and a network for completing object occupancy. Its implicit shape decoder supports occupancy volumes of varying size. The network uses temporal information from long sequences to predict complete shapes even when the object proposals supplied to it are inaccurate.

Experiments report robust shape completion under noisy detection and tracking conditions. The learned occupancy features also significantly improve state-of-the-art 3D detectors on the Waymo Open Dataset, particularly for distant or incompletely observed objects. The approach therefore connects detailed object reconstruction with better detection, while directing high-resolution representation toward the parts of the scene where object geometry is needed.
neurips-2024-towards-flexible-3d-percept.tldr: Object-centric occupancy completion adds detailed shapes to bounding boxes and improves 3D detection, especially for distant or incomplete objects.

paragraphs: A pretrained model can be useful for a new task, but success is difficult to predict when both the domain and the task change. This paper studies representation transfer through task-relatedness. It compares downstream tasks with a reference task to explain when pretrained knowledge is likely to support strong target performance.

The analysis produces an upper bound on transferability expressed through differences in class priors, label sets, and features. These components make relatedness more specific than a general notion of task similarity. The proposed quantity can also be computed efficiently without target-task labels, making it applicable when labeled evidence for evaluating candidate models is unavailable.

Experiments with state-of-the-art pretrained models across vision and language tasks show that task-relatedness helps explain transfer behavior. It correlates strongly with accuracy after end-to-end target-task fine-tuning. The authors also demonstrate its practical use in selecting a pretrained model from a model zoo. Together, the theoretical bound and empirical results support relatedness as an estimator for model selection, with correlation providing the reported empirical evidence.
neurips-2024-understanding-the-transfera.tldr: A task-relatedness measure combines label, class-prior, and feature differences to explain transferability and help select pretrained models.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization chooses a predictor by minimizing error on training data. This paper studies its learning curves: how expected error decreases as the number of examples grows. It uses the universal learning framework, motivated by differences between universal and uniform rates that the classical PAC perspective does not fully explain.

The analysis focuses on the realizable setting, where the concept class can represent the target. Its main result separates universal learning by empirical risk minimization into four possible rate categories: exponential decay of the form e⁻ⁿ, decay at 1/n, decay at log(n)/n, or arbitrarily slow decay. This provides a structural classification of possible learning behavior under the studied assumptions.

The authors introduce complexity structures that completely characterize which concept classes belong to each category. They also develop combinatorial dimensions giving sharp asymptotic constant factors where possible. The contribution goes beyond identifying several example rates: it specifies the possible categories and connects membership in them to properties of the class being learned.
neurips-2024-universal-rates-of-empirica.tldr: In the realizable universal-learning setting, empirical risk minimization has four possible rate categories characterized by concept-class structure.

paragraphs: Business process management includes documenting, measuring, improving, and automating workflows. This paper argues that model evaluation has concentrated too heavily on end-to-end automation, overlooking work such as documentation that occupies much of a typical process optimization project. WONDERBREAD broadens evaluation to tasks that support people in understanding and improving enterprise processes.

The benchmark contains 2,928 documented workflow demonstrations, six tasks drawn from real applications, and an automated evaluation harness. Its tasks cover areas including workflow documentation, knowledge transfer, and process improvement. This combination supplies demonstrations and evaluation tasks for studying several uses of multimodal foundation models within business process management.

The results reveal a gap between describing a workflow and checking its execution. Models can generate documentation that recalls 88% of the steps in a video demonstration, yet struggle with detailed validation of workflow completion, reporting F1 below 0.3. The finding shows why documentation ability alone is insufficient evidence for reliable completion checking and motivates evaluating these capabilities separately.
neurips-2024-wonderbread-a-benchmark-for.tldr: WONDERBREAD evaluates workflow tasks beyond automation and finds a substantial gap between generating documentation and validating completion.

paragraphs: Joint-embedding architectures have achieved strong self-supervised learning results using extensive handcrafted data augmentation. This history has encouraged the belief that those transformations are required for effective training. The paper tests that belief at scale, asking whether strong representations can emerge with a much simpler augmentation setup when enough training data is available.

The authors conduct a case study using DINOv2. They show that a joint-embedding architecture trained with cropping alone, without resizing, can learn strong image representations and reach state-of-the-art results provided the dataset is sufficiently large. The data-scale condition is central to the finding: the reported success concerns a simplified training setup supported by enough data.

The study also examines how computational constraints influence conclusions in experimental deep learning. Results obtained under different resource budgets can support very different interpretations of which ingredients are necessary. The contribution challenges the assumed dependence on strong domain-specific augmentation and shows why conclusions about training requirements should be understood in relation to the scale at which they were tested.
neurips-2024-you-dont-need-domain-specif.tldr: A DINOv2 case study achieves strong representations with cropping alone when training data is sufficiently large.
